prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a discovery-level idea with an exceptionally sharp realisation. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal makes the light shift of the trap cancel for the clock transition, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with neither Doppler nor recoil broadening. Ye's group then showed that this many-atom architecture, with spin-polarised strontium, cavity-stabilised lasers and frequency-comb links, could reach systematic uncertainties near 1e-18. The result is mature: independent groups at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere have reproduced it across Sr, Yb and Hg, and intercontinental comparisons exist. The physics is also still productive, in relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, and in the ongoing roadmap to redefine the second. The adjacent comb and ion-trap contributions were recognised in 2005 and 2012, so the credit boundary is comparatively clean and a two-person prize is coherent.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a lattice clock is partly an engineering refinement of ideas already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and some colleagues may see it as incremental next to a new window on the Universe or a completed Standard Model. Attribution beyond Katori and Ye is also not fully closed: Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others made real contributions to the Sr clock, and Lemonde in particular is outside the credited list. If the committee weighs the broad consequences for fundamental physics more heavily than precision and instrumental originality, B026 or B053 could reasonably outrank it.

responses.point: Kroll also ranks optical lattice clocks first and stresses that Katori made the decisive magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, while Ye took the clock to record accuracy and added many-body and cavity-stabilised-laser developments, so a two-person prize is clean.
responses.response: I agree on the pairing, and two further points reinforce it from where I stand. Reaching 1e-18 required controlling the atomic structure side: blackbody-radiation shifts, higher-order light shifts and hyperpolarisability. Those are the parts that made the many-atom lattice a real clock rather than a good idea. I would not agree, though, that agreement among us on this ballot is evidence of merit. Three of us ranked it first, and Kroll and I share an atomic-physics vantage that could make us overweight precision metrology. The test is whether colleagues outside AMO find the conceptual step substantial, so I would rather have that argued than assumed.

responses.point: Danielsson places the experimental Higgs discovery first, as a decisive result that completed the Standard Model, with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as the natural trio of founding proposers and leaders of the detector programmes.
responses.response: I accept the scientific weight completely, and the discovery is the more consequential result for the field as a whole. My reservation is attribution. A prize for a discovery made by thousands, credited to three founding leaders, rests on an argument about leadership rather than about who made the decisive scientific step, and the committee has not agreed to that standard. It also follows a 2013 prize that already recognised the theory. I would keep B026 as a strong alternative, and if colleagues can settle a defensible attribution basis I would reconsider. As it stands, B042 has a more identifiable origin and a clearer credit list.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for opening neutrino astronomy, with Halzen and Spiering as the pioneers of the kilometre-scale detector, and notes that source identification is still partial though the diffuse flux is robustly confirmed.
responses.response: The diffuse flux is firmly established, and a two-name prize for Halzen and Spiering is feasible. I share Pearce's own caveat, though, that the astrophysical interpretation is still developing, and the Baikal, ANTARES and DUMAND pioneers complicate the credit boundary. Against optical clocks, IceCube is the less settled on maturity, and I read Pearce's emphasis on detector achievement as an argument for instrument-driven prizes, which also favours the lattice clock. I would not put B029 in my top configuration, but I do not think it is far off, and a good paper on source identification in the next years could change that.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first on the grounds that it underlies dispersive readout, gates and bus architectures in essentially every superconducting processor, and notes that the four-name credit forces an uncomfortable choice between Blais and Girvin.
responses.response: The impact on quantum technology is undeniable and the strong-coupling experiments were a real step. Two things hold me back. First, the credit list has four names for a three-person limit, and dropping Blais or Girvin is not a decision I can make on scientific grounds. Second, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits has just covered closely neighbouring ground, and I would want some distance before recognising the same platform again. I think the two proposals are less far apart than the rankings suggest, and I would put circuit QED and the Cirac-Zoller ion-trap work together as the main quantum-technology alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a configuration for B042 that excludes Pierre Lemonde, Takamoto and other early Sr-clock contributors, given that the credited list contains only Katori and Ye.
How far members outside atomic physics regard the lattice clock as a conceptual advance rather than an incremental refinement of the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes.
Whether the Higgs experimental discovery (B026) can be given a defensible attribution under the three-person limit; if it can, it may outrank B042 on overall scientific consequence.
Whether the thorium-229 nuclear-clock work or a possible redefinition of the second will change the timing argument either way.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile for B042: it documents no collaboration, supervision or institutional tie with Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye. I disclose that I work in theoretical atomic physics and have documented collaborations with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato. None of these is a shortlisted credited name here, but I would flag the connection if a ballot concerning attosecond physics came up. My field proximity to optical clocks is a matter of expertise rather than a documented personal connection.
